To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

elevated extracellular potassium concentrations and monoamine agonists exert a complex and different effect on the energy metabolism in the different cell types of the CNS, and that these effects are important for the understanding of the role of the CNS cells in neurotransmission and in the regulation of extracellular ion composition.

(1) excess K+ stimulates neuronal-astrocyte interaction by stimulating metabolic events involved in the promotion of neuronal transmitter production and the reestablishment of neuronal ion homeostasis; and (2) the adrenergic transmitters stimulate energy metabolism in astrocytic cells in a complex manner, and, in so
the stimulation of brain energy production by excess K+ is more pronounced than by monoamine transmitters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic processes in astrocytes that are stimulated by the neurotransmitters, and with the role of these processes in the regulation of neuronal function.
the question of whether and how the brain can respond to the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation and to the effects of monoamine transmitters.
the metabolic effects of excess K+ and monoamines on different cell types and on different sub-cellular structures in the CNS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
excess K+ stimulates neuronal energy production and ion transport and that monoamine transmitters enhance astrocytic energy metabolism and ion transport.
the effects of excess K+ and of monoamines are different in different cell types and that the effects on neurons and glial cells are also different.
the monoamines and excess K+ stimulate different processes in astrocytes, and that these processes are not identical with those stimulated in the neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
excess K+ stimulates energy production in both neurons and astrocytes, whereas monoamines stimulate energy production in astrocytes but not in neurons.
the metabolic effects of K+ and monoamine transmittors on brain metabolism appear to be different in astrocytes and in neurons.
excess K+ and adrenergic transmitters stimulate different cellular metabolic processes, which in turn may have profound implications for the regulation of neurotransmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of elevated K+, and of adrenergic and cholinergic agonists on brain energy metabolism are highly specific for cell type and for subcellular structure and that the metabolic processes stimulated by these agents are different in neurons and astrocytes.
the metabolic effects of excess K+ and monoamines on neurons and astrocytes are very different.
the metabolic effects of elevated K+, noradrenaline, or dopamine are highly selective, and the metabolic effects of excess K+ are quite different from those of adrenergic transmitters.
